props.name: forId
props.description: The `id` of the control this label names. Required for the same reason Link's `href` is: a label with no `for` is a mistake the compiler catches, and passing `""` explicitly is the visible way to say "decorative label".  Named `for`, not `htmlFor`. Stencil maps a camelCase prop to its kebab attribute (`htmlFor` → `html-for`), so a consumer writing the HTML attribute `for` — the only spelling that exists in plain markup — would set nothing, and the label would silently associate with nothing. The first build proved it: `for="standalone-email"` in the page, `for=""` in the DOM. The native `for` attribute name is also what `Element.prototype` reserves, so a prop named `for` would collide with it — hence `for` as the *attribute* via `@Prop({ attribute: "for" })` on a differently-named field.

props.name: marker
props.description: Where the marker sits. `before` reads naturally for checkboxes and switches, where the control leads the sentence.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the labeled control as required and renders the marker.  This sets `aria-required` on **this** element, not the control — the consumer sets `required` on the control itself, and the label marking the control on its behalf would be a second component reaching into another's DOM, which §4 forbids.

ai.summary: A programmatic label for any control: names it through `for`, and clicking it focuses the control through the browser's own activation.
whenToUse: A control was built without its own label and needs one that is actually associated
A checkbox or switch needs its marker before the text, where the control leads the sentence
A custom field needs the same label record Input's built-in label uses
whenNotToUse: The control already has a label prop — Input and Textarea wire their own; two labels for one control is a bug
It would label nothing — `for` is required; a label with no control is a span with ambition, use plain text
The text describes a group of controls — use a Fieldset or a heading, not a label
ai.accessibility: Associates through `htmlFor` pointing at the control's id, so clicking the label focuses the control via the browser's own activation — no click handler here, because the platform's is better and reimplementing it means reimplementing its edge cases. The required marker is `aria-hidden`: the control's own `required` attribute carries the semantics, the asterisk is for the sighted, and color alone never carries it (WCAG 1.4.1). `required` here does not set anything on the control — a label reaching into another component's DOM is exactly what section 4 forbids.
knownLimitations: Field components render their control with the id `${hostId}-control`, so `for` must carry that suffix — a cross-component id contract is tracked as open
It cannot label a control rendered inside a shadow root it cannot see — `for` must match a light-DOM id
It does not generate ids; pair it with the control's own id or React's `useId()`
